'''Warren Arthur Ambrose''' (October 25, 1914 – December 4, 1995) was Professor Emeritus of Mathematics at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] and at the [[University of Buenos Aires]].

He was born in [[Virden, Illinois]] in 1914. He received his bachelor of science degree in 1935, his master's in 1936 and his [[Ph.D.]] in 1939, all from the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]].<ref name=mit>{{cite web|url=http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/1996/ambrose-0110.html |title=Professor Emeritus Warren Ambrose dies at 81 - MIT News Office |publisher=Web.mit.edu |date=1996-01-10 |accessdate=2012-09-28}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Warren Ambrose was a food and wine connoisseur, and also a fan of jazz saxophone player, [[Charlie Parker|Charlie "Bird" Parker]]. He is noted for his work with MIT colleague, [[Isadore Singer]], both of whom helped to shape the pure mathematics department at MIT.<ref name=ams>{{cite web|url=http://www.ams.org/notices/199604/comm-ambrose.pdf |title=A Tribute to Warren Ambrose - I. M. Singer and H. Wu |date= |accessdate=2012-09-28}}</ref> He retired from teaching at MIT in 1985, thereafter moving to [[France]]. Ambrose died in 1995 in [[Paris]]. He was survived by his wife, Jeannette (Grillet) Ambrose of Paris, two children from an earlier marriage, Adam Ambrose of Bisbee, AZ, and Ellen Ambrose of Laurel, MD, and four grandchildren,<ref name=mit/> David and Adam Holzsager, Ari Ambrose, and Jennifer Laurent.

== Career ==
Ambrose became an assistant professor at MIT in 1947, an associate professor in 1950 and full professor in 1957.<ref name=mit/> He was several times between 1939 and 1959 a visiting scholar at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in  [[Princeton, New Jersey]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ias.edu/people/cos/frontpage?page=3 |title=Institute for Advanced Study: A Community of Scholars |publisher=Ias.edu |accessdate=2012-09-28 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20130106144327/http://www.ias.edu/people/cos/frontpage?page=3 |archivedate=2013-01-06 }}</ref> Ambrose is often considered one of the fathers of modern geometry.<ref name=reflections>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3P0IQDorWEoC&pg=PA111 |title=Reflections Of Eminent Economists - Michael Szenberg, Lall Ramrattan - Google Books |date= January 2004|isbn=9781845423636 |accessdate=2012-09-28|last1=Szenberg |first1=Michael |last2=Ramrattan |first2=Lall |publisher=Edward Elgar }}</ref> He is noted for making changes in the pure mathematics undergraduate curriculum at MIT to reflect recent findings in differential geometry. For example, less than ten years after André Weil presented the differential form, Ambrose was using it in his undergraduate differential geometry courses.  In the 1950s, Ambrose (together with I. M. Singer) made MIT into the only center in geometry in the United States outside the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name=ams/> His influence continued through his students, in particular [[Hung-Hsi Wu]] and [[John Rhodes (mathematician)|John Rhodes]], both of the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. In the 1960s Ambrose was a visiting professor at the [[University of Buenos Aires]], [[Argentina]]. He is noted for his opposition of takeover of South American countries military regimes, specifically Argentina.<ref name=mit/>

== Political activism ==
In the summer of 1966, while a visiting professor at the University of Buenos Aires in Argentina, Ambrose was severely beaten along with Argentinian faculty members and students by Argentinian military police. This occurred shortly after a military regime took over public universities in Argentina. Ambrose responded by bringing several of the best and brightest students from the University of Buenos Aires back to MIT with him.<ref name=reflections/> Ambrose is often renowned amongst Latin American intellectuals for bringing attention to right-wing dictatorships in South America.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HP6CYnCbHOEC&q=warren+ambrose+MIT&pg=PA17 |title=The Man Who Pushed America to War: The Extraordinary Life, Adventures, and ... - Aram Roston - Google Books |date= 24 February 2009|isbn=9781568584157 |accessdate=2012-09-28|last1=Roston |first1=Aram |publisher=PublicAffairs }}</ref>

In 1967, Ambrose signed a letter declaring his intention to [[tax resistance|refuse to pay taxes]] in protest against the U.S. war against Vietnam, and urging other people to also take this stand.<ref>"An Open Letter" [http://collection1.libraries.psu.edu/cdm/singleitem/collection/transaction/id/17162 archived at Horowitz Transaction Publishers Archive] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130619122110/http://collection1.libraries.psu.edu/cdm/singleitem/collection/transaction/id/17162 |date=2013-06-19 }}</ref>
